name: Willow bark extract

card.summary: A salicin-rich herbal extract with some oral trial data for back and joint pain, but essentially no trials as a skin ingredient.
card.aka: White willow bark, Salix alba extract, salicin source
card.note: Contains salicylate precursors; the evidence cited is for oral pain use, not appearance.

quick.overview:
Willow bark extract comes from Salix species and contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylate. It has a long history as a traditional pain and fever remedy and is the historical source of salicylic acid chemistry.
Skincare brands sometimes use it as a 'natural salicylic acid' for acne or exfoliation. The clinical trials found are all oral studies in pain conditions, so skin claims are untested in those sources.
quick.mechanism: Salicin is a glucoside; after ingestion it is metabolised to salicylic acid derivatives. Reviews note that polyphenols and flavonoids in the extract may also contribute to anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.risks: Salicylates are toxic in excess, and salicylate-containing products carry labelled cautions. Topical cosmetic willow extracts have little dedicated safety literature.

lead: Willow bark extract is a preparation from the bark of willow trees, most often white willow (Salix alba), containing the glucoside salicin along with polyphenols and flavonoids.[1][2] Salicin was isolated in crystalline form in 1828, and salicylic acid is derived from it chemically.[1][3]

For appearance, it appears in two ways. Skincare brands promote it as a plant-derived source of salicylic-acid-like action for blemish-prone, oily skin and enlarged pores, and one 2024 trial tested an emulsion containing white willow bark extract on acne and facial pores.[3][9] In the gym and joint-care world it is taken orally for back and joint discomfort, and through less pain and inflammation people aim to keep training, which is the chain behind its use in sports and physique supplements.[2][4][5][16]
Published human trials of the oral extract concern low back pain and osteoarthritis; trials of topical willow bark as a single skin ingredient have not been found.

paras: In 1763 Edward Stone of Oxfordshire reported using powdered willow bark to treat fevers in about fifty people over several years, though Wikipedia notes the medical profession largely ignored this at the time.[1] Salicin was isolated by Henri Leroux and Raffaele Piria in 1828, while Wikipedia's salicylic acid entry credits Johann Andreas Buchner that year; Piria later obtained salicylic acid from it.[1][3] Aspirin itself is a synthetic derivative and does not occur in nature.[1] A 2015 review notes that willow bark has been used for thousands of years as an anti-inflammatory, antipyretic and analgesic.[2]

Skincare brands describe willow bark extract as a gentler plant-derived alternative to salicylic acid for blemish-prone skin. Salicylic acid itself is an established keratolytic used for acne and other skin conditions,[3] but no trials show that willow bark extract in a topical product delivers comparable effects. It also shows up in combination products, such as an emulsion with niacinamide and lens esculenta seed extract that was evaluated for oily skin and enlarged pores over 56 days.[9]

The 2015 review notes that willow bark extracts are widely used in sports performance and weight loss products presumably for anti-inflammatory and analgesic activity, though no human studies directly document benefits for those purposes.[2] Bodybuilding forum threads show it in joint-support blends alongside glucosamine, chondroitin and turmeric, and in older stimulant fat-burner formulas; one poster credited such a joint blend with relieving a knee problem over about three months.[18][19] Posters also describe it as the natural counterpart of aspirin, and another commenter in a separate thread characterised it as acting like aspirin and able to mask more serious problems.[20][21]

Oral standardised extracts are used in Europe for low back pain and osteoarthritis.[4][5] A 2002 review of herbal antirheumatics reports that a particular willow bark extract providing 120 to 240 mg salicin daily showed efficacy in clinical studies.[10]

Salicin is a glucoside; after ingestion it is metabolised to salicylic acid and its derivatives, and a pharmacokinetic study in ten healthy volunteers measured salicylic acid and its metabolites gentisic acid and salicyluric acid in serum and urine after a standardised extract.[3][11] Unlike aspirin, salicin and its metabolites lack acetylating potential, and an analysis of the aqueous extract STW 33-I concluded that salicin content alone does not satisfactorily explain clinical effect, pointing to contributions from the polyphenol and flavonoid fractions.[12] In vitro and animal work associates the extract's anti-inflammatory activity with down-regulation of tumour necrosis factor-alpha and nuclear factor-kappa B, and a 2005 paper studied further mechanisms of a standardised extract.[2][13] A 2013 study reported increased antioxidant enzymes through Nrf2 activation in endothelial cells and C. elegans.[14]

A randomised double-blind study enrolled 210 patients with exacerbations of chronic low back pain and tested an oral willow bark extract.[4] Another randomised study compared a herbal and a synthetic anti-rheumatic for low back pain.[15] A systematic review of musculoskeletal pain identified seven manuscripts reporting four confirmatory and four exploratory trials: one confirmatory and two exploratory studies indicated a dose-dependent analgesic effect not inferior to rofecoxib in low back pain, results in osteoarthritis were conflicting, and a grossly underpowered study in rheumatoid arthritis showed no significant effect; minor adverse events occurred and the authors described moderate evidence for ethanolic extracts at up to 240 mg salicin daily for up to six weeks.[6] A placebo-controlled trial and two further randomised trials examined osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, and systematic reviews of herbal anti-inflammatory drugs also exist.[5][7][17]

A 2015 review concluded that a small number of clinical studies support its use in chronic low back and joint pain and osteoarthritis, while noting that relatively few human and animal studies have been published.[2] A 2024 clinical trial evaluated a multi-ingredient emulsion containing niacinamide, lens esculenta seed extract and white willow bark extract for oily skin, acne and conspicuous pores over 56 days.[9] A registered trial of a multi-ingredient product listing Salix alba studied anxiety, not skin.[8] No studies of topical willow bark extract alone for appearance were found.

The 2015 review states that adverse effects appear minimal compared with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including aspirin, while noting a primary area of concern, and Wikipedia notes that salicylates in excess are toxic.[2][3] One cited study judged cosmetic salicylic acid use not to pose significant systemic risk, and the pure acid carries hazards such as eye damage.[3] A commenter on a bodybuilding forum describes willow bark as acting like aspirin in the body and advises raising it with a doctor.[21] A US supplement label containing white willow bark extract is on file with DailyMed.[22]

chain: Extract supplies salicin, a salicylate precursor, plus polyphenols
Topically: salicylic-acid-style effect on oily, blemish-prone skin is the claim; orally: less joint and back pain
Clearer-looking skin, or more comfortable training
angle.text: Cosmetic brands use willow bark extract as a gentler botanical stand-in for salicylic acid on oily or blemish-prone skin, and athletes take it orally for joint and back discomfort so they can keep training.
